1 Corinthians — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)

The church at Corinth included some Jews but more Gentiles.

Paul had to confront Jewish religious superstition on one hand and Gentile believers' sinful conduct on the other.

The church's peace was disturbed by false teachers who undermined the apostle's influence.

This produced two opposing groups.

One insisted strongly upon Jewish ceremonies.

The other tolerated excesses opposed to the gospel, encouraged by the luxury and sins widespread in Corinth.

Paul wrote this letter for two purposes.

First, he intended to correct the disorderly conduct and abuses that had been reported to him.

Second, he wanted to give satisfactory answers to questions upon which Corinthian believers had requested his judgment.

It is remarkable how Paul combined Christian gentleness with firmness, moving from general truths directly toward correction of the church's errors and sins.

He explained God's truth and will about different matters with powerful arguments and an energetic style.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesA salutation and thanksgiving.1–9Exhortation to brotherly love, and reproof for divisions.10–16The doctrine of a crucified Saviour, as advancing the glory of God,17–25and humbling the creature before him.26–31
Paul's greeting and thanksgiving (verses 1–9)

Through baptism, people who profess Christianity are dedicated to Christ and obligated to holiness.

But the true church of God consists of those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints, and who call upon Christ as God manifested in human flesh for every blessing of salvation.

They acknowledge and obey him as their Lord and the Lord of all.

This is what marks genuine members of his church.

Christians are distinguished from those who disregard God by the fact that they cannot live without prayer.

They are distinguished from Jews and pagans in that they call upon the name of Jesus Christ.

Notice how frequently Paul names our Lord Jesus Christ in these verses.

He was not afraid to speak of Christ often or give him too much honor.

To everyone calling on Christ, Paul offered his familiar greeting of grace and peace.

He desired that God's mercy would pardon them, his grace would sanctify them and his peace would comfort them, all through Jesus Christ.

Sinners have no peace with God and receive no true peace from him apart from Christ.

Paul thanked God for their conversion and for the grace Christ had given them.

They had been enriched with spiritual gifts, including speech and knowledge.

When God gives both, he provides great opportunities to be useful.

These gifts were works of the Holy Spirit, through which God confirmed the apostles' witness.

Those waiting for Jesus' return will be preserved by him to the end and declared blameless at his appearing through rich and freely given grace.

What a glorious hope—to be kept by Christ's power against inward corruption and Satan's temptations!

Paul calls the church away from division (verses 10–16)

In the central truths of religion, believers should agree in understanding.

Where opinions still differ, they should remain united in affection.

Agreement in major matters should outweigh disputes about lesser ones.

There will be perfect unity in heaven.

The closer believers approach that unity here, the closer they come to Christian maturity.

Paul and Apollos were both faithful servants of Christ, helping believers in faith and joy.

But contentious people organized themselves into rival factions.

Even the best institutions can be corrupted: the gospel itself may be misused as a weapon for quarrelling.

Satan has always treated division among Christians as one of his chief methods of opposing the gospel.

Paul allowed other ministers to perform most baptisms while he focused on preaching, which he regarded as the more useful task entrusted to him.

Christ crucified reveals divine wisdom (verses 17–25)

Paul had received extensive Jewish learning.

Yet the plain preaching of Jesus crucified proved more powerful than the combined rhetoric and philosophy of the pagan world.

This is the heart of the gospel.

Christ crucified is the foundation of our hope and the source of our joy.

Through his death we live.

Preaching that lost sinners are saved through the suffering and death of God's Son seems foolish to those moving toward destruction.

People controlled by sensuality, greed, pride or ambition recognize that the gospel threatens the pursuits they love.

But those who receive the gospel and are enlightened by the Holy Spirit discover more divine wisdom and power in the crucified Christ than in any other work of God.

God allowed much of the world to follow the guidance of its proudly asserted human wisdom.

History shows that this wisdom could not discover or preserve a right knowledge of God the Creator.

God chose to save believers through what the worldly call the foolishness of preaching.

This does not mean preaching that deserves to be called foolish.

Rather, the message of Christ appears foolish to people proud of worldly wisdom.

Plain proclamation of Christ continues to distinguish those responding to God's saving grace from those refusing it.

The world despises salvation by faith in a crucified Savior, who is God in human nature and purchased the church with his own blood.

Yet God has used that message through every generation to save multitudes who believe, freeing them from ignorance, deception and wickedness.

Even the weakest instruments God employs are more effective than humanity's greatest natural strength.

There is no foolishness or weakness in God.

What people call foolish or weak defeats their most admired wisdom and power.

God chooses the lowly to humble human pride (verses 26–31)

God did not chiefly choose the world's philosophers, eloquent speakers, political leaders or wealthy and influential figures to proclaim his gospel.

He knows which people and methods most serve his glory.

Not many noble people are called, but some have been called in every age.

They too need forgiveness, and some have gladly confessed Christ despite their status.

A humble believer who possesses little wealth or formal education may understand the gospel better than a scholar who studies Scripture merely as human writing instead of the word of God.

Even children have sometimes understood divine truths well enough to answer unbelievers.

The reason is that God himself taught them.

The purpose is that no human being should boast before him.

Our relationship to Christ does not arise from our own wisdom or effort.

Through God's sovereign choice and regenerating grace we are brought into Jesus Christ by faith.

Christ becomes for us wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption.

He gives us everything we need or could rightly desire.

As Wisdom, through his word and Spirit, Christ teaches us from the fullness of his knowledge and makes us wise for salvation and service.

As Righteousness, he is the atoning sacrifice for guilty sinners deserving judgment.

As Sanctification, he remedies our fallen corruption.

And as Redemption, he will finally free the soul from all sin and the body from the grave.

All this fulfills the word of Jeremiah 9:23–24, that every person should boast only in the Lord's favor, sufficient grace and precious salvation.
classic_reading:
[1Cor.1.1-1Cor.1.9]
1 Corinthians
The Corinthian church contained some Jews, but more Gentiles, and the apostle had to contend with the superstition of the one, and the sinful conduct of the other. The peace of this church was disturbed by false teachers, who undermined the influence of the apostle. Two parties were the result; one contending earnestly for the Jewish ceremonies, the other indulging in excesses contrary to the gospel, to which they were especially led by the luxury and the sins which prevailed around them. This epistle was written to rebuke some disorderly conduct, of which the apostle had been apprized, and to give advice as to some points whereon his judgment was requested by the Corinthians. Thus the scope was twofold. 1. To apply suitable remedies to the disorders and abuses which prevailed among them. 2. To give satisfactory answers on all the points upon which his advice had been desired. The address, and Christian mildness, yet firmness, with which the apostle writes, and goes on from general truths directly to oppose the errors and evil conduct of the Corinthians, is very remarkable. He states the truth and the will of God, as to various matters, with great force of argument and animation of style.
Chapter 1
Chapter Outline
A salutation and thanksgiving. | (1-9) |
Exhortation to brotherly love, and reproof for divisions. | (10-16) |
The doctrine of a crucified Saviour, as advancing the glory of God,
(17-25)
and humbling the creature before him.
(26-31)
Verses 1-9
All Christians are by baptism dedicated and devoted to Christ, and are under strict obligations to be holy. But in the true church of God are all who are sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints, and who call upon him as God manifest in the flesh, for all the blessings of salvation; who acknowledge and obey him as their Lord, and as Lord of all; it includes no other persons. Christians are distinguished from the profane and atheists, that they dare not live without prayer; and they are distinguished from Jews and pagans, that they call on the name of Christ. Observe how often in these verses the apostle repeats the words, Our Lord Jesus Christ. He feared not to make too frequent or too honourable mention of him. To all who called upon Christ, the apostle gave his usual salutation, desiring, in their behalf, the pardoning mercy, sanctifying grace, and comforting peace of God, through Jesus Christ. Sinners can have no peace with God, nor any from him, but through Christ. He gives thanks for their conversion to the faith of Christ; that grace was given them by Jesus Christ. They had been enriched by him with all spiritual gifts. He speaks of utterance and knowledge. And where God has given these two gifts, he has given great power for usefulness. These were gifts of the Holy Ghost, by which God bore witness to the apostles. Those that wait for the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, will be kept by him to the end; and those that are so, will be blameless in the day of Christ, made so by rich and free grace. How glorious are the hopes of such a privilege; to be kept by the power of Christ, from the power of our corruptions and Satan's temptations!
[1Cor.1.10-1Cor.1.16]
Verses 10-16
In the great things of religion be of one mind; and where there is not unity of sentiment, still let there be union of affection. Agreement in the greater things should extinguish divisions about the lesser. There will be perfect union in heaven, and the nearer we approach it on earth, the nearer we come to perfection. Paul and Apollos both were faithful ministers of Jesus Christ, and helpers of their faith and joy; but those disposed to be contentious, broke into parties. So liable are the best things to be corrupted, and the gospel and its institutions made engines of discord and contention. Satan has always endeavoured to stir up strife among Christians, as one of his chief devices against the gospel. The apostle left it to other ministers to baptize, while he preached the gospel, as a more useful work.
[1Cor.1.17-1Cor.1.25]
Verses 17-25
Paul had been bred up in Jewish learning; but the plain preaching of a crucified Jesus, was more powerful than all the oratory and philosophy of the heathen world. This is the sum and substance of the gospel. Christ crucified is the foundation of all our hopes, the fountain of all our joys. And by his death we live. The preaching of salvation for lost sinners by the sufferings and death of the Son of God, if explained and faithfully applied, appears foolishness to those in the way to destruction. The sensual, the covetous, the proud, and ambitious, alike see that the gospel opposes their favourite pursuits. But those who receive the gospel, and are enlightened by the Spirit of God, see more of God's wisdom and power in the doctrine of Christ crucified, than in all his other works. God left a great part of the world to follow the dictates of man's boasted reason, and the event has shown that human wisdom is folly, and is unable to find or retain the knowledge of God as the Creator. It pleased him, by the foolishness of preaching, to save them that believe. By the foolishness of preaching; not by what could justly be called foolish preaching. But the thing preached was foolishness to wordly-wise men. The gospel ever was, and ever will be, foolishness to all in the road to destruction. The message of Christ, plainly delivered, ever has been a sure touchstone by which men may learn what road they are travelling. But the despised doctrine of salvation by faith in a crucified Saviour, God in human nature, purchasing the church with his own blood, to save multitudes, even all that believe, from ignorance, delusion, and vice, has been blessed in every age. And the weakest instruments God uses, are stronger in their effects, than the strongest men can use. Not that there is foolishness or weakness in God, but what men consider as such, overcomes all their admired wisdom and strength.
[1Cor.1.26-1Cor.1.31]
Verses 26-31
God did not choose philosophers, nor orators, nor statesmen, nor men of wealth, and power, and interest in the world, to publish the gospel of grace and peace. He best judges what men and what measures serve the purposes of his glory. Though not many noble are usually called by Divine grace, there have been some such in every age, who have not been ashamed of the gospel of Christ; and persons of every rank stand in need of pardoning grace. Often, a humble Christian, though poor as to this world, has more true knowledge of the gospel, than those who have made the letter of Scripture the study of their lives, but who have studied it rather as the witness of men, than as the word of God. And even young children have gained such knowledge of Divine truth as to silence infidels. The reason is, they are taught of God; the design is, that no flesh should glory in his presence. That distinction, in which alone they might glory, was not of themselves. It was by the sovereign choice and regenerating grace of God, that they were in Jesus Christ by faith. He is made of God to us wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption; all we need, or can desire. And he is made wisdom to us, that by his word and Spirit, and from his fulness and treasures of wisdom and knowledge, we may receive all that will make us wise unto salvation, and fit for every service to which we are called. We are guilty, liable to just punishment; and he is made righteousness, our great atonement and sacrifice. We are depraved and corrupt, and he is made sanctification, that he may in the end be made complete redemption; may free the soul from the being of sin, and loose the body from the bonds of the grave. And this is, that all flesh, according to the prophecy by Jeremiah, [Jer.9.23-Jer.9.24] Jer 9:23-24, may glory in the special favour, all-sufficient grace, and precious salvation of Jehovah.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe plain manner in which the apostle preached Christ crucified.1–5The wisdom contained in this doctrine.6–9It cannot be duly known but by the Holy Spirit.10–16
Paul's plain preaching of Christ crucified (verses 1–5)

Jesus Christ—his person, offices and sufferings—is the heart of the gospel.

He should be the main subject of every gospel minister's preaching.

This does not mean leaving out other parts of God's revealed truth and will.

Paul proclaimed the whole counsel of God.

Few people understand the fear and trembling experienced by faithful ministers who recognize their own weakness.

They know how inadequate their abilities are and feel their responsibility deeply.

When ministers simply proclaim Christ crucified, any genuine saving success must come from God's power accompanying his word.

Through that power, sinners believe and receive salvation.

God's deep wisdom revealed in Christ (verses 6–9)

Those who receive the gospel as divine truth and examine it under the Holy Spirit's light see more than the outward historical facts about Jesus' crucifixion.

They recognize God's deep and wonderful plan of wisdom.

This is the mystery now revealed to the saints (Colossians 1:26).

It had been hidden from the pagan world and only dimly pictured by Old Testament types and distant prophecies.

Now the Spirit of God has disclosed it.

Jesus is the Lord of glory, a title too exalted for any merely created being.

Many people would not oppose God's saving work if they truly understood his wisdom in redemption.

God has prepared blessings for those who love and wait for him that bodily senses cannot discover and human teaching cannot fully convey.

We cannot yet imagine their greatness.

We must receive these promises as they are revealed to us in Scripture.

The Holy Spirit enables spiritual understanding (verses 10–16)

God reveals true wisdom through his Holy Spirit.

This helps demonstrate the divine authority of Scripture (2 Peter 1:21).

It also bears witness to the deity of the Holy Spirit.

He knows and searches all things, even the depths of God.

No one can know God's inner purposes except his Spirit, who is one with the Father and the Son and reveals divine mysteries to the church.

Henry sees here testimony to the Holy Spirit's true deity and distinct personhood.

The apostles were not governed by worldly principles.

They received revelation of these truths through God's Spirit, together with the Spirit's saving impact upon them.

They communicated them in plain language taught by the Holy Spirit, instead of relying upon artificial rhetoric or manipulative human eloquence.

The natural person, even when regarded by the world as wise, does not receive the things of God's Spirit.

Pride in worldly reasoning can oppose spiritual truth as strongly as the crudest sensuality.

A mind sanctified by God recognizes the beauty of holiness.

This does not destroy its ability to reason about ordinary natural affairs.

But the unregenerate person does not understand the principles, pleasures and activity of divine life.

Only the spiritual person receives from God the knowledge of his saving will.

How little people understand of God's mind through merely natural powers!

The apostles received the Spirit's help to disclose it.

The mind of Christ, and God's mind as revealed in Christ, are made known in the Holy Scriptures.

Christians are privileged to receive that revelation through the Spirit, experience his sanctifying work within and bear good fruit in life.
classic_reading:
[1Cor.2.1-1Cor.2.5]
Chapter 2
Chapter Outline
The plain manner in which the apostle preached Christ crucified. | (1-5) |
The wisdom contained in this doctrine. | (6-9) |
It cannot be duly known but by the Holy Spirit. | (10-16) |
Verses 1-5
Christ, in his person, and offices, and sufferings, is the sum and substance of the gospel, and ought to be the great subject of a gospel minister's preaching, but not so as to leave out other parts of God's revealed truth and will. Paul preached the whole counsel of God. Few know the fear and trembling of faithful ministers, from a deep sense of their own weakness They know how insufficient they are, and are fearful for themselves. When nothing but Christ crucified is plainly preached, the success must be entirely from Divine power accompanying the word, and thus men are brought to believe, to the salvation of their souls.
[1Cor.2.6-1Cor.2.9]
Verses 6-9
Those who receive the doctrine of Christ as Divine, and, having been enlightened by the Holy Spirit, have looked well into it, see not only the plain history of Christ, and him crucified, but the deep and admirable designs of Divine wisdom therein. It is the mystery made manifest to the saints, [Col.1.26] Col 1:26, though formerly hid from the heathen world; it was only shown in dark types and distant prophecies, but now is revealed and made known by the Spirit of God. Jesus Christ is the Lord of glory; a title much too great for any creature. There are many things which people would not do, if they knew the wisdom of God in the great work of redemption. There are things God hath prepared for those that love him, and wait for him, which sense cannot discover, no teaching can convey to our ears, nor can it yet enter our hearts. We must take them as they stand in the Scriptures, as God hath been pleased to reveal them to us.
[1Cor.2.10-1Cor.2.16]
Verses 10-16
God has revealed true wisdom to us by his Spirit. Here is a proof of the Divine authority of the Holy Scriptures, [2Pet.1.21] 2Pe 1:21. In proof of the Divinity of the Holy Ghost, observe, that he knows all things, and he searches all things, even the deep things of God. No one can know the things of God, but his Holy Spirit, who is one with the Father and the Son, and who makes known Divine mysteries to his church. This is most clear testimony, both to the real Godhead and the distinct person of the Holy Spirit. The apostles were not guided by worldly principles. They had the revelation of these things from the Spirit of God, and the saving impression of them from the same Spirit. These things they declared in plain, simple language, taught by the Holy Spirit, totally different from the affected oratory or enticing words of man's wisdom. The natural man, the wise man of the world, receives not the things of the Spirit of God. The pride of carnal reasoning is really as much opposed to spirituality, as the basest sensuality. The sanctified mind discerns the real beauties of holiness, but the power of discerning and judging about common and natural things is not lost. But the carnal man is a stranger to the principles, and pleasures, and actings of the Divine life. The spiritual man only, is the person to whom God gives the knowledge of his will. How little have any known of the mind of God by natural power! And the apostles were enabled by his Spirit to make known his mind. In the Holy Scriptures, the mind of Christ, and the mind of God in Christ, are fully made known to us. It is the great privilege of Christians, that they have the mind of Christ revealed to them by his Spirit. They experience his sanctifying power in their hearts, and bring forth good fruits in their lives.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe Corinthians reproved for their contentions.1–4The true servants of Christ can do nothing without him.5–9He is the only foundation, and every one should take heed what he builds thereon.10–15The churches of Christ ought to be kept pure, and to be humble.16, 17And they should not glory in men, because ministers and all things else are theirs through Christ.18–23
Quarreling reveals spiritual immaturity (verses 1–4)

Simple gospel truths about human sin, God's mercy, repentance toward God and faith in Jesus Christ benefit many believers more than difficult mysteries.

A person may know a great deal about Christian doctrine yet remain a beginner in living faith and spiritual experience.

Arguments and quarrels over religion reveal remaining worldliness and immaturity.

True religion makes people peaceable rather than contentious.

Sadly, many professing Christians continue behaving too much like the surrounding world.

Some believers—and even ministers—show carnality through boastful rivalry, eagerness to dispute and willingness to despise or insult others.

Ministers are servants; only God produces growth (verses 5–9)

The ministers over whom the Corinthians fought were only instruments God had chosen to use.

We must never put ministers in God's place.

The person planting and the person watering belong to one work.

Both serve the same Lord, receive the same revelation and pursue the same purpose.

Their different gifts come from the same Holy Spirit and should be used in sincere cooperation.

Those who work diligently and faithfully will receive God's reward.

They cooperate in God's work to advance his glory and the salvation of souls.

The Lord knows their labor and will ensure it has not been wasted.

They are workers in God's field and God's building, both of which remain under his careful supervision.

Christ is the only foundation (verses 10–15)

Paul was a wise builder, but God's grace made him one.

Spiritual pride is especially shameful because it turns the Lord's greatest gifts into fuel for our vanity and self-idolatry.

Every Christian worker must be careful.

A person can build poorly upon a good foundation.

Only things consistent with the foundation should be placed upon it.

We must not combine a merely worldly life with divine faith or join sinful practices to a claim of Christianity.

Jesus Christ is the firm, unchanging Rock of Ages.

He can bear every burden God places upon him and every burden the sinner brings to him.

There is salvation in no one else.

Remove Christ's atonement, and the foundation of Christian hope disappears.

Among those who profess to build on Christ, Henry describes two kinds of workers.

Some proclaim the truth as it is in Jesus and build only what agrees with that truth.

Others build things that cannot survive the coming test, though they profess the same good foundation.

We may misjudge ourselves or others.

But a day is coming when every work will be seen in its true light, without disguise.

Those whose work spreads true and pure religion will receive a reward, far greater than they deserve.

Other workers' corrupt teachings, human inventions and unauthorized religious practices will be exposed and rejected.

The fire that tests these works is figurative, not literal fire.

No ordinary flame can consume a doctrine or a religious ceremony.

The test applies to everyone's work, including Paul and Apollos.

Let us consider the effects of our undertakings, compare them with Scripture and judge ourselves, so that God need not condemn our work.

God's church must remain holy (verses 16 and 17)

Elsewhere in the letter we learn that some Corinthian false teachers promoted unholy ideas.

Such instruction threatened to corrupt and destroy God's building, which should be preserved pure.

People spreading doctrines that encourage an unholy church bring judgment upon themselves.

Christ dwells by his Spirit within genuine believers.

Christians profess to be holy and should therefore seek purity in heart and conduct.

Anyone who believes themselves to be a temple of the Holy Spirit while remaining indifferent to personal holiness and the church's peace and purity is deceived.

Do not boast in human wisdom or ministers (verses 18–23)

Having an exaggerated opinion of our own wisdom is self-flattery, and self-flattery leads quickly to self-deception.

The wisdom admired by the world is foolishness before God.

He can easily confound its supposed experts.

Even the thoughts of the most intelligent humans contain weakness, error and emptiness.

This should humble us and make us eager to learn from God.

Do not let claims of human expertise turn you from the plain truth revealed by Christ.

Human beings often resist the very purposes for which God blesses them.

Consider the spiritual wealth of true believers: “All things are yours.”

Ministers and appointed means of grace serve their good.

Even the world belongs to them in the sense that infinite divine wisdom gives them as much of it as is good for them, together with God's blessing.

Life belongs to believers as time to prepare for eternity.

Death belongs to them as a messenger bringing them from sin and sorrow to their Father's house.

Present things sustain them during the journey.

Future things will delight them forever at its end.

If we belong to Christ, all truly good things are secure for us.

Believers are subjects of his kingdom.

He is our Lord, and we ought to accept his authority gladly.

God in Christ reconciling sinful people to himself and pouring out grace upon them is the heart of the gospel.
classic_reading:
[1Cor.3.1-1Cor.3.4]
Chapter 3
Chapter Outline
The Corinthians reproved for their contentions.
(1-4)
The true servants of Christ can do nothing without him.
(5-9)
He is the only foundation, and every one should take heed what he builds thereon.
(10-15)
The churches of Christ ought to be kept pure, and to be humble.
(16-17)
And they should not glory in men, because ministers and all things else are theirs through Christ.
(18-23)
Verses 1-4
The most simple truths of the gospel, as to man's sinfulness and God's mercy, repentance towards God, and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, stated in the plainest language, suit the people better than deeper mysteries. Men may have much doctrinal knowledge, yet be mere beginners in the life of faith and experience. Contentions and quarrels about religion are sad evidences of carnality. True religion makes men peaceable, not contentious. But it is to be lamented, that many who should walk as Christians, live and act too much like other men. Many professors, and preachers also, show themselves to be yet carnal, by vain-glorious strife, eagerness for dispute, and readiness to despise and speak evil of others.
[1Cor.3.5-1Cor.3.9]
Verses 5-9
The ministers about whom the Corinthians contended, were only instruments used by God. We should not put ministers into the place of God. He that planteth and he that watereth are one, employed by one Master, trusted with the same revelation, busied in one work, and engaged in one design. They have their different gifts from one and the same Spirit, for the very same purposes; and should carry on the same design heartily. Those who work hardest shall fare best. Those who are most faithful shall have the greatest reward. They work together with God, in promoting the purposes of his glory, and the salvation of precious souls; and He who knows their work, will take care they do not labour in vain. They are employed in his husbandry and building; and He will carefully look over them.
[1Cor.3.10-1Cor.3.15]
Verses 10-15
The apostle was a wise master-builder; but the grace of God made him such. Spiritual pride is abominable; it is using the greatest favours of God, to feed our own vanity, and make idols of ourselves. But let every man take heed; there may be bad building on a good foundation. Nothing must be laid upon it, but what the foundation will bear, and what is of a piece with it. Let us not dare to join a merely human or a carnal life with a Divine faith, the corruption of sin with the profession of Christianity. Christ is a firm, abiding, and immovable Rock of ages, every way able to bear all the weight that God himself or the sinner can lay upon him; neither is there salvation in any other. Leave out the doctrine of his atonement, and there is no foundation for our hopes. But of those who rest on this foundation, there are two sorts. Some hold nothing but the truth as it is in Jesus, and preach nothing else. Others build on the good foundation what will not abide the test, when the day of trail comes. We may be mistaken in ourselves and others; but there is a day coming that will show our actions in the true light, without covering or disguise. Those who spread true and pure religion in all its branches, and whose work will abide in the great day, shall receive a reward. And how great! how much exceeding their deserts! There are others, whose corrupt opinions and doctrines, or vain inventions and usages in the worship of God, shall be made known, disowned, and rejected, in that day. This is plainly meant of a figurative fire, not of a real one; for what real fire can consume religious rites or doctrines? And it is to try every man's works, those of Paul and Apollos, as well as others. Let us consider the tendency of our undertakings, compare them with God's word, and judge ourselves, that we be not judged of the Lord.
[1Cor.3.16-1Cor.3.17]
Verses 16-17
From other parts of the epistle, it appears that the false teachers among the Corinthians taught unholy doctrines. Such teaching tended to corrupt, to pollute, and destroy the building, which should be kept pure and holy for God. Those who spread loose principles, which render the church of God unholy, bring destruction upon themselves. Christ by his Spirit dwells in all true believers. Christians are holy by profession, and should be pure and clean, both in heart and conversation. He is deceived who deems himself the temple of the Holy Ghost, yet is unconcerned about personal holiness, or the peace and purity of the church.
[1Cor.3.18-1Cor.3.23]
Verses 18-23
To have a high opinion of our own wisdom, is but to flatter ourselves; and self-flattery is the next step to self-deceit. The wisdom that wordly men esteem, is foolishness with God. How justly does he despise, and how easily can he baffle and confound it! The thoughts of the wisest men in the world, have vanity, weakness, and folly in them. All this should teach us to be humble, and make us willing to be taught of God, so as not to be led away, by pretences to human wisdom and skill, from the simple truths revealed by Christ. Mankind are very apt to oppose the design of the mercies of God. Observe the spiritual riches of a true believer; "All are yours," even ministers and ordinances. Nay, the world itself is yours. Saints have as much of it as Infinite Wisdom sees fit for them, and they have it with the Divine blessing. Life is yours, that you may have a season and opportunity to prepare for the life of heaven; and death is yours, that you may go to the possession of it. It is the kind messenger to take you from sin and sorrow, and to guide you to your Father's house. Things present are yours, for your support on the road; things to come are yours, to delight you for ever at your journey's end. If we belong to Christ, and are true to him, all good belongs to us, and is sure to us. Believers are the subjects of his kingdom. He is Lord over us, we must own his dominion, and cheerfully submit to his command. God in Christ, reconciling a sinful world to himself, and pouring the riches of his grace on a reconciled world, is the sum and substance of the gospel.

Ministers are servants entrusted with Christ's work (verses 1–6)

The apostles were servants of Christ, and should never be treated as if they were their Master. Yet they should not be undervalued, because the Lord had entrusted them with something of extraordinary importance. Their calling was honorable precisely because of this responsibility.

Paul rightly cared about his reputation. But someone whose chief ambition is to please other people cannot remain a faithful servant of Christ.

It is a comfort that human beings will not be our final judges.

Nor can we make ourselves safe simply by giving ourselves a favorable verdict. Our judgment of our faithfulness is no more dependable than our own works are sufficient to justify us before God.

A day is approaching when everything now concealed will be brought into the light. People's hidden sins and the secrets of their hearts will be disclosed.

Then every believer wrongly slandered will be vindicated, and every faithful servant will be approved and rewarded.

For now, God's word is our best standard for judging people and their conduct.

Pride frequently lies beneath quarrels. The same self-importance that leads us to admire ourselves too highly can also make us give excessive honor to the teachers we prefer.

We will not become inflated in favor of one leader against another if we remember that all ministers are instruments appointed by God and equipped with gifts from him.

The apostles' sufferings expose worldly boasting (verses 7–13)

We have no grounds for pride.

Everything genuinely good in who we are, what we possess and what we do comes from God's rich, freely given grace.

It would be absurd for a sinner rescued from destruction by sovereign mercy to boast about gifts received from that mercy.

Paul described the apostles' circumstances by an image drawn from the cruel spectacles of the Roman games (verse 9).

Men were compelled to fight one another for the crowd's entertainment. Even a victor who survived one fight was kept for another, until eventually he too would be killed.

Believers should remember that many eyes are upon them when they struggle with trouble or temptation. Such knowledge should encourage faithfulness and patience.

Paul wrote, “We are weak, but you are strong.”

Christians do not all experience the same trials. Some endure much greater hardships than others.

The apostles suffered in body and reputation. They were treated like the most contemptible people on earth, the dirt swept away and the refuse discarded.

Yet love for Christ and devotion to his work carried them through their suffering.

Everyone determined to be faithful to Jesus must be prepared for poverty and contempt, if these come.

Christ's disciples are called to follow his example and obey his commands even when the world despises or mistreats them.

It is far better to be rejected as Paul was than to possess the world's approval while abandoning Christ.

Those regarded by the world as worthless may be precious to God. He will receive them and grant them a place with him.

Correction should be loving and spiritually effective (verses 14–21)

When correcting wrongdoing, distinguish between the person and the sin.

A loving and affectionate warning is more likely to lead to genuine reform than a harsh rebuke.

Although Paul could speak with a father's authority, he preferred to appeal to the Corinthians in love.

Ministers should provide an example, and believers should imitate them only insofar as they imitate Christ in faith and conduct.

Christians may misunderstand matters or differ in their opinions. Yet Christ and the truth he has revealed remain the same yesterday, today and forever.

Where the gospel is truly effective, it comes not only in words but also in the power of the Holy Spirit.

The Spirit gives life to sinners who were spiritually dead.

He releases people from slavery to sin and Satan, renews them inwardly and outwardly, and comforts, strengthens and establishes the saints.

Persuasive human speech cannot accomplish these things. They require God's power.

It is a blessed disposition when love and gentleness govern our conduct while we still exercise the rightful authority entrusted to us.

[1Cor.4.1-1Cor.4.6]
Chapter 4
Chapter Outline
The true character of gospel ministers. | (1-6) |
Cautions against despising the apostle. | (7-13) |
He claims their regard as their spiritual father in Christ, and shows his concern for them. | (14-21) |
Verses 1-6
Apostles were no more than servants of Christ, but they were not to be undervalued. They had a great trust, and for that reason, had an honourable office. Paul had a just concern for his own reputation, but he knew that he who chiefly aimed to please men, would not prove himself a faithful servant of Christ. It is a comfort that men are not to be our final judges. And it is not judging well of ourselves, or justifying ourselves, that will prove us safe and happy. Our own judgment is not to be depended upon as to our faithfulness, any more than our own works for our justification. There is a day coming, that will bring men's secret sins into open day, and discover the secrets of their hearts. Then every slandered believer will be justified, and every faithful servant approved and rewarded. The word of God is the best rule by which to judge as to men. Pride commonly is at the bottom of quarrels. Self-conceit contributes to produce undue esteem of our teachers, as well as of ourselves. We shall not be puffed up for one against another, if we remember that all are instruments, employed by God, and endowed by him with various talents.
[1Cor.4.7-1Cor.4.13]
Verses 7-13
We have no reason to be proud; all we have, or are, or do, that is good, is owing to the free and rich grace of God. A sinner snatched from destruction by sovereign grace alone, must be very absurd and inconsistent, if proud of the free gifts of God. St. Paul sets forth his own circumstances, ver. 9 Allusion is made to the cruel spectacles in the Roman games; where men were forced to cut one another to pieces, to divert the people; and where the victor did not escape with his life, though he should destroy his adversary, but was only kept for another combat, and must be killed at last. The thought that many eyes are upon believers, when struggling with difficulties or temptations, should encourage constancy and patience. "We are weak, but ye are strong." All Christians are not alike exposed. Some suffer greater hardships than others. The apostle enters into particulars of their sufferings. And how glorious the charity and devotion that carried them through all these hardships! They suffered in their persons and characters as the worst and vilest of men; as the very dirt of the world, that was to be swept away: nay, as the offscouring of all things, the dross of all things. And every one who would be faithful in Christ Jesus, must be prepared for poverty and contempt. Whatever the disciples of Christ suffer from men, they must follow the example, and fulfil the will and precepts of their Lord. They must be content, with him and for him, to be despised and abused. It is much better to be rejected, despised, and ill used, as St. Paul was, than to have the good opinion and favour of the world. Though cast off by the world as vile, yet we may be precious to God, gathered up with his own hand, and placed upon his throne.
[1Cor.4.14-1Cor.4.21]
Verses 14-21
In reproving for sin, we should distinguish between sinners and their sins. Reproofs that kindly and affectionately warn, are likely to reform. Though the apostle spoke with authority as a parent, he would rather beseech them in love. And as ministers are to set an example, others must follow them, as far as they follow Christ in faith and practice. Christians may mistake and differ in their views, but Christ and Christian truth are the same yesterday, to-day, and for ever. Whenever the gospel is effectual, it comes not in word only, but also in power, by the Holy Spirit, quickening dead sinners, delivering persons from the slavery of sin and Satan, renewing them both inwardly and outwardly, and comforting, strengthening, and establishing the saints, which cannot be done by the persuasive language of men, but by the power of God. And it is a happy temper, to have the spirit of love and meekness bear the rule, yet to maintain just authority.

The church must not tolerate scandalous sin (verses 1–8)

Paul exposed a shameful abuse that the Corinthian church had overlooked.

It seems that party loyalty and a mistaken view of Christian liberty had protected the offender from correction.

It is grievous when professing Christians commit crimes that even unbelievers would be ashamed to commit.

Spiritual pride and false teaching encourage these scandals and allow them to spread.

How terrible sin's effects can be!

Satan rules wherever Christ does not rule. Anyone who remains outside Christ's kingdom remains under Satan's power.

The example of an influential person can do exceptional harm, spreading widely through the community.

Corrupt principles and sinful practices, if left uncorrected, can harm the whole church.

Believers need new hearts and new lives.

Both their everyday conduct and their religious worship must be holy.

The sacrifice of Christ our Passover does not make personal or communal holiness unnecessary.

On the contrary, his sacrifice supplies the strongest reasons and motives for pursuing it.

Without holiness, we can neither live by genuine faith in Christ nor benefit comfortably and fruitfully from the ordinances he has appointed.

Avoid close fellowship with those who dishonor Christ's name (verses 9–13)

Christians should avoid close and familiar fellowship with those who openly disgrace the Christian name while claiming to belong to him.

People persisting in such conduct should, as far as possible, be left to the companionship of others who follow the same sins.

It is a sorrowful fact that some people called Christians are more dangerous companions than those who openly remain outside the faith.

The church must not let outward profession conceal openly scandalous behavior.

Settle disputes as brothers and sisters (verses 1–8)

Christians ought not to quarrel with one another, because they are brothers and sisters in Christ.

If they gave this relationship proper weight, many lawsuits, arguments and disputes would never begin.

Where serious injury to ourselves or our families is involved, we may use lawful means to obtain justice.

Paul's instruction should not be turned into an absolute ban on seeking legal redress.

Nevertheless, believers should have a forgiving disposition.

Whenever possible, they should refer disputes to trustworthy people among their fellow believers instead of bringing every disagreement into court.

Many disagreements are small enough to be settled readily if we first conquer our own passions.

Learn to bear with each other and yield where appropriate.

Even people of limited learning and experience may be able to settle quarrels if the parties are prepared to listen.

It is shameful when minor disputes among Christians become so bitter that no one among them can help reconcile them.

Peace within one's own mind and tranquillity among neighbors are worth more than winning a case.

When lawsuits occur between believers, something has already gone wrong in their relationships.

Grace changes people who once practiced serious sins (verses 9–11)

Paul warned the Corinthians against numerous grave sins, including sins in which some of them had formerly lived.

This warning carried particular force because the Corinthians had become proud of their supposed knowledge and wisdom.

All unrighteousness is sin.

Any sin deliberately practiced and left unrepented—any sin allowed to reign—shuts a person out of God's kingdom.

Do not deceive yourselves.

People naturally flatter themselves with the idea that they can live in sin, die belonging to Christ and enjoy heaven.

But no one can sow to the flesh and reap eternal life.

Paul reminded the Corinthian Christians of the tremendous change the gospel and God's grace had produced in them.

Christ's blood and the washing of regeneration can remove all sin's guilt.

Our justification comes from the suffering and merit of Jesus Christ.

Our sanctification comes from the Holy Spirit's work.

These two graces are inseparably joined: everyone made righteous before God is also made holy by God's grace.

Believers' bodies belong to Christ (verses 12–20)

Some Corinthians appear to have argued that everything was lawful for them.

Paul opposed this dangerous idea.

Christ has truly set believers free, and they should remain firm in that liberty.

But no Christian should willingly become a slave to any bodily appetite.

Our bodies belong to the Lord.

They are meant to serve as instruments of righteousness leading to holiness, not instruments of sin.

Jesus Christ's resurrection brought honor to his body.

The future resurrection will also bring glory to believers' bodies.

The hope of that resurrection should encourage Christians to refuse sexual immorality and other practices that dishonor the body.

The believer's soul is united to Christ through faith.

Therefore the whole person becomes a member of his spiritual body.

Some sins may be resisted through direct struggle, but sexual immorality must be fled.

Its destructive consequences have ruined many lives.

Its harm affects not only the body but often the mind.

Christ redeemed our bodies from deserved condemnation and hopeless slavery through his atoning sacrifice.

We must keep them clean as vessels suitable for our Master's use.

United to Christ as one spirit and purchased at a price of immeasurable value, we belong wholly to him.

May we spend the rest of our lives, until the final day and hour, glorifying God with our bodies and our spirits, which are his.

[1Cor.6.1-1Cor.6.8]
Chapter 6
Chapter Outline
Cautions against going to law in heathen courts. | (1-8) |
Sins which, if lived and died in, shut out from the kingdom of God. | (9-11) |
Our bodies, which are the members of Christ, and temples of the Holy Ghost, must not be defiled. | (12-20) |
Verses 1-8
Christians should not contend with one another, for they are brethren. This, if duly attended to, would prevent many law-suits, and end many quarrels and disputes. In matters of great damage to ourselves or families, we may use lawful means to right ourselves, but Christians should be of a forgiving temper. Refer the matters in dispute, rather than go to law about them. They are trifles, and may easily be settled, if you first conquer your own spirits. Bear and forbear, and the men of least skill among you may end your quarrels. It is a shame that little quarrels should grow to such a head among Christians, that they cannot be determined by the brethren. The peace of a man's own mind, and the calm of his neighbourhood, are worth more than victory. Lawsuits could not take place among brethren, unless there were faults among them.
[1Cor.6.9-1Cor.6.11]
Verses 9-11
The Corinthians are warned against many great evils, of which they had formerly been guilty. There is much force in these inquiries, when we consider that they were addressed to a people puffed up with a fancy of their being above others in wisdom and knowledge. All unrighteousness is sin; all reigning sin, nay, every actual sin, committed with design, and not repented of, shuts out of the kingdom of heaven. Be not deceived. Men are very much inclined to flatter themselves that they may live in sin, yet die in Christ, and go to heaven. But we cannot hope to sow to the flesh, and reap everlasting life. They are reminded what a change the gospel and grace of God had made in them. The blood of Christ, and the washing of regeneration, can take away all guilt. Our justification is owing to the suffering and merit of Christ; our sanctification to the working of the Holy Spirit; but both go together. All who are made righteous in the sight of God, are made holy by the grace of God.
[1Cor.6.12-1Cor.6.20]
Verses 12-20
Some among the Corinthians seem to have been ready to say, All things are lawful for me. This dangerous conceit St. Paul opposes. There is a liberty wherewith Christ has made us free, in which we must stand fast. But surely a Christian would never put himself into the power of any bodily appetite. The body is for the Lord; is to be an instrument of righteousness to holiness, therefore is never to be made an instrument of sin. It is an honour to the body, that Jesus Christ was raised from the dead; and it will be an honour to our bodies, that they will be raised. The hope of a resurrection to glory, should keep Christians from dishonouring their bodies by fleshly lusts. And if the soul be united to Christ by faith, the whole man is become a member of his spiritual body. Other vices may be conquered in fight; that here cautioned against, only by flight. And vast multitudes are cut off by this vice in its various forms and consequences. Its effects fall not only directly upon the body, but often upon the mind. Our bodies have been redeemed from deserved condemnation and hopeless slavery by the atoning sacrifice of Christ. We are to be clean, as vessels fitted for our Master's use. Being united to Christ as one spirit, and bought with a price of unspeakable value, the believer should consider himself as wholly the Lord's, by the strongest ties. May we make it our business, to the latest day and hour of our lives, to glorify God with our bodies, and with our spirits which are his.

Paul answered questions the Corinthians had raised about marriage.

He considered it good for some Christians to remain unmarried under the particular circumstances of that time.

Yet marriage and its blessings have been established by God's wisdom.

No one may break his law. Within its perfect requirements, however, God grants freedom to serve him in ways suited to people's different abilities and circumstances.

Other people are often poor judges of these circumstances.

Each Christian should consider personal responsibilities and seek God's counsel before deciding.

Marriage to an unbelieving spouse (verses 10–16)

A husband and wife should not separate except on grounds Christ permits.

Divorce was common among Jews and Gentiles in Paul's time, sometimes for the smallest reasons.

But marriage is God's institution, appointed as a lasting commitment.

We are to pursue peace with all people, insofar as it depends upon us (Romans 12:18).

How much more should we seek the comfort and peace of those closest to us, even if a spouse does not share Christian faith!

Married people should make it a serious aim to promote each other's happiness.

Why should someone professing Christ abandon a husband or wife when that relationship offers a particularly important opportunity to show genuine love?

Stay and work earnestly for the conversion of your spouse, where remaining in the marriage is the duty God has given.

In every calling and relationship, God has called believers to peace.

Do everything possible to maintain harmony, as far as truth and holiness permit.

Serve Christ faithfully in your present condition (verses 17–24)

Christianity reaches people in every social position and circumstance.

Someone can honor the gospel through faithful conduct in any lawful occupation or place.

Christians should be content with the position assigned to them and behave in a way that reflects their faith.

Our happiness depends on what we are in relation to Christ, not what we are in the world's eyes.

Faith must not be used as an excuse to abandon natural or civil responsibilities.

Normally believers should carry out their existing duties quietly and contentedly, trusting divine Providence.

Live with eternal priorities in troubled times (verses 25–35)

Considering the troubles facing believers at that time, remaining unmarried could be preferable.

Paul did not thereby condemn marriage.

How contrary to his instruction are those who forbid marriage to large groups of people or bind them with vows of celibacy regardless of whether this calling suits them!

Paul encouraged Christians to hold the things of this world loosely.

In personal relationships, do not set your heart entirely on their comforts.

In suffering, do not let worldly grief dominate, because joy in God remains possible even amid sorrow.

In earthly pleasures, remember that they are not your final rest.

In business, even when trade prospers and wealth increases, hold possessions as though they were not your ultimate property or hope.

In every worldly concern, keep the world from ruling your heart, so you will not misuse its gifts when they are placed in your hands.

All earthly things are temporary appearances.

Nothing here lasts.

Prudent attention to practical responsibilities is a duty.

But anxious and overwhelming preoccupation with them is wrong.

The best calling for a person is the one that most benefits that person's soul and best guards against worldly traps and distractions.

Examine the advantages and dangers of your circumstances. Use the former wisely and avoid the latter as much as possible.

Whatever legitimate responsibilities occupy you, always preserve time for the Lord's concerns.

Wise decisions about marriage and widowhood (verses 36–40)

Henry explains that Paul is understood by some to be discussing the responsibility of parents when arranging marriages for their children.

On this reading, children should seek and normally follow parental guidance in choosing a spouse.

But parents must also consult their children's wishes.

Parents do not have unlimited power to dictate such a lifelong decision without good reasons or regard for their children.

Paul concludes with advice to widows.

Remarriage is not unlawful, provided it is undertaken in the Lord.

In choosing close relationships and considering a change in circumstances, we should be governed by reverence for God, his commands and dependence upon his Providence.

classic_reading:
[1Cor.7.1-1Cor.7.9]
Chapter 7
Chapter Outline
The apostle answers several questions about marriage.
(1-9)
Married Christians should not seek to part from their unbelieving consorts.
(10-16)
Persons, in any fixed station, should usually abide in that.
(17-24)
It was most desirable, on account of the then perilous days, for people to sit loose to this world.
(25-35)
Great prudence be used in marriage; it should be only in the Lord.
(36-40)
Verses 1-9
The apostle tells the Corinthians that it was good, in that juncture of time, for Christians to keep themselves single. Yet he says that marriage, and the comforts of that state, are settled by Divine wisdom. Though none may break the law of God, yet that perfect rule leaves men at liberty to serve him in the way most suited to their powers and circumstances, of which others often are very unfit judges. All must determine for themselves, seeking counsel from God how they ought to act.
[1Cor.7.10-1Cor.7.16]
Verses 10-16
Man and wife must not separate for any other cause than what Christ allows. Divorce, at that time, was very common among both Jews and Gentiles, on very slight pretexts. Marriage is a Divine institution; and is an engagement for life, by God's appointment. We are bound, as much as in us lies, to live peaceably with all men, [Rom.12.18] Ro 12:18, therefore to promote the peace and comfort of our nearest relatives, though unbelievers. It should be the labour and study of those who are married, to make each other as easy and happy as possible. Should a Christian desert a husband or wife, when there is opportunity to give the greatest proof of love? Stay, and labour heartily for the conversion of thy relative. In every state and relation the Lord has called us to peace; and every thing should be done to promote harmony, as far as truth and holiness will permit.
[1Cor.7.17-1Cor.7.24]
Verses 17-24
The rules of Christianity reach every condition; and in every state a man may live so as to be a credit to it. It is the duty of every Christian to be content with his lot, and to conduct himself in his rank and place as becomes a Christian. Our comfort and happiness depend on what we are to Christ, not what we are in the world. No man should think to make his faith or religion, an argument to break through any natural or civil obligations. He should quietly and contentedly abide in the condition in which he is placed by Divine Providence.
[1Cor.7.25-1Cor.7.35]
Verses 25-35
Considering the distress of those times, the unmarried state was best. Notwithstanding, the apostle does not condemn marriage. How opposite are those to the apostle Paul who forbid many to marry, and entangle them with vows to remain single, whether they ought to do so or not! He exhorts all Christians to holy indifference toward the world. As to relations; they must not set their hearts on the comforts of the state. As to afflictions; they must not indulge the sorrow of the world: even in sorrow the heart may be joyful. As to worldly enjoyments; here is not their rest. As to worldly employment; those that prosper in trade, and increase in wealth, should hold their possessions as though they held them not. As to all worldly concerns; they must keep the world out of their hearts, that they may not abuse it when they have it in their hands. All worldly things are show; nothing solid. All will be quickly gone. Wise concern about worldly interests is a duty; but to be full of care, to have anxious and perplexing care, is a sin. By this maxim the apostle solves the case whether it were advisable to marry. That condition of life is best for every man, which is best for his soul, and keeps him most clear of the cares and snares of the world. Let us reflect on the advantages and snares of our own condition in life; that we may improve the one, and escape as far as possible all injury from the other. And whatever cares press upon the mind, let time still be kept for the things of the Lord.
[1Cor.7.36-1Cor.7.40]
Verses 36-40
The apostle is thought to give advice here about the disposal of children in marriage. In this view, the general meaning is plain. Children should seek and follow the directions of their parents as to marriage. And parents should consult their children's wishes; and not reckon they have power to do with them, and dictate just as they please, without reason. The whole is closed with advice to widows. Second marriages are not unlawful, so that it is kept in mind, to marry in the Lord. In our choice of relations, and change of conditions, we should always be guided by the fear of God, and the laws of God, and act in dependence on the providence of God. Change of condition ought only to be made after careful consideration, and on probable grounds, that it will be to advantage in our spiritual concerns.

Knowledge without love produces pride (verses 1–6)

Nothing proves ignorance more commonly than a conceited opinion of one's own knowledge.

A person may know many facts yet know nothing in the way that truly matters.

Those who become proud of what they understand are often the least likely to use it well.

Satan harms some people through pride in intellectual powers, just as he tempts others through bodily pleasures.

Knowledge that makes people arrogant, self-confident and dismissive of others is just as dangerous as self-righteous pride, even when the information itself is accurate.

Without holy love and godly affections, all our knowledge is worthless.

The pagans worshiped many beings they called gods or lords, some considered greater and others lesser.

But none was God in truth.

Christians know the one God who created everything and rules over everything.

Paul speaks of one God, the Father, as the Godhead who alone is the rightful object of all religious worship.

He also speaks of one Lord, Jesus Christ: Emmanuel, God manifested in flesh, one with the Father and united with us.

Christ is the appointed Mediator and Lord of all.

Through him we come to the Father, and through him the Father gives us every spiritual blessing by the Holy Spirit's power and work.

We must refuse religious worship not only to idols, but also to creatures wrongly treated as divine, including saints and angels.

Above all, examine yourselves: do you truly approach God through faith in Christ?

Do not harm weaker believers through careless liberty (verses 7–13)

Eating a particular kind of food or abstaining from it does not make a person acceptable before God.

Yet Paul warns against creating a stumbling block for a weaker believer.

Someone with a sensitive conscience might imitate a person who knows an idol is nothing.

But instead of eating the food simply as ordinary food, the weaker believer might eat it as an offering to the idol, becoming guilty of idolatry.

The distinction matters.

A person possessing Christ's Spirit will love people whom Christ loved enough to die for them.

Injuries done to Christians are done to Christ himself.

The most serious injury is entangling them in sin and wounding their consciences.

Christians must be especially careful not to put others in a position where they may stumble, even through an act harmless in itself.

If we must guard other people's souls in this way, how much more carefully should we protect our own!

Avoid moving unnecessarily close to evil or even its appearance.

Many people excuse such risks in public life by arguments that sound plausible.

But no one can sin against a brother or sister without offending Christ and endangering their own soul.
classic_reading:
[1Cor.8.1-1Cor.8.6]
Chapter 8
Chapter Outline
The danger of having a high conceit of knowledge. | (1-6) |
The mischief of offending weak brethren. | (7-13) |
Verses 1-6
There is no proof of ignorance more common than conceit of knowledge. Much may be known, when nothing is known to good purpose. And those who think they know any thing, and grow vain thereon, are the least likely to make good use of their knowledge. Satan hurts some as much by tempting them to be proud of mental powers, as others, by alluring to sensuality. Knowledge which puffs up the possessor, and renders him confident, is as dangerous as self-righteous pride, though what he knows may be right. Without holy affections all human knowledge is worthless. The heathens had gods of higher and lower degree; gods many, and lords many; so called, but not such in truth. Christians know better. One God made all, and has power over all. The one God, even the Father, signifies the Godhead as the sole object of all religious worship; and the Lord Jesus Christ denotes the person of Emmanuel, God manifest in the flesh, One with the Father, and with us; the appointed Mediator, and Lord of all; through whom we come to the Father, and through whom the Father sends all blessings to us, by the influence and working of the Holy Spirit. While we refuse all worship to the many who are called gods and lords, and to saints and angels, let us try whether we really come to God by faith in Christ.
[1Cor.8.7-1Cor.8.13]
Verses 7-13
Eating one kind of food, and abstaining from another, have nothing in them to recommend a person to God. But the apostle cautions against putting a stumbling-block in the way of the weak; lest they be made bold to eat what was offered to the idol, not as common food, but as a sacrifice, and thereby be guilty of idolatry. He who has the Spirit of Christ in him, will love those whom Christ loved so as to die for them. Injuries done to Christians, are done to Christ; but most of all, the entangling them in guilt: wounding their consciences, is wounding him. We should be very tender of doing any thing that may occasion stumbling to others, though it may be innocent in itself. And if we must not endanger other men's souls, how much should we take care not to destroy our own! Let Christians beware of approaching the brink of evil, or the appearance of it, though many do this in public matters, for which perhaps they plead plausibly. Men cannot thus sin against their brethren, without offending Christ, and endangering their own souls.

It is nothing new for ministers to receive unkind treatment in return for good intentions, diligent work and fruitful service.

He was not required to earn all this through his own manual labor.

Those who care for our souls should receive provision for their bodily needs.

Yet Paul deliberately surrendered this right rather than allow demanding his support to hinder the gospel's work.

The duty of supporting gospel ministers nevertheless remains with the people they serve.

A minister may waive a right, as Paul did.

But congregations who deny or withhold the support due to ministers violate Christ's command.

Paul gives up liberty to win people for Christ (verses 15–23)

It is a minister's honor to deny personal advantage in order to serve Christ and lead people to salvation.

When a minister voluntarily gives up lawful support for the gospel's sake, that person goes beyond the minimum required by the office.

By preaching without payment, Paul showed his zeal and love.

This gave him encouragement and hope in his own soul.

He understood that the ceremonial law had become a yoke removed by Christ.

Yet he was willing to comply with its observances where this could help Jewish hearers overcome prejudice, listen to the gospel and be brought to Christ.

He never broke Christ's commandments merely to please people.

But wherever lawful, he adapted his conduct to those he served, seeking to win at least some.

Doing good was the great work of his life.

He refused to let insistence upon personal privileges obstruct that goal.

We must guard against extremes and trust Christ alone, rather than our own flexible conduct, for salvation.

And we must never tolerate error or misconduct that injures others or brings disgrace upon the gospel.

Run the race for an unfading crown (verses 24–27)

Paul drew upon the races and athletic contests held at the Isthmian games, familiar to the Corinthians.

In the Christian race, everyone may run in such a way as to obtain the prize.

This is powerful encouragement to persevere with all our strength.

The contestants followed strict diets, trained their bodies, became accustomed to hardship and practiced their skills.

Similarly, those concerned for their eternal welfare must fight against sinful bodily desires.

The body must not be allowed to govern the soul.

Paul urged believers to beware of indulging appetite or giving in to temptation.

He himself recognized the danger of yielding to the desires of the flesh.

[1Cor.9.1-1Cor.9.14]
Chapter 9
Chapter Outline
The apostle shows his authority, and asserts his right to be maintained.
(1-14)
He waved this part of his Christian liberty, for the good of others.
(15-23)
He did all this, with care and diligence, in view of an unfading crown.
(24-27)
Verses 1-14
It is not new for a minister to meet with unkind returns for good-will to a people, and diligent and successful services among them. To the cavils of some, the apostle answers, so as to set forth himself as an example of self-denial, for the good of others. He had a right to marry as well as other apostles, and to claim what was needful for his wife, and his children if he had any, from the churches, without labouring with his own hands to get it. Those who seek to do our souls good, should have food provided for them. But he renounced his right, rather than hinder his success by claiming it. It is the people's duty to maintain their minister. He may wave his right, as Paul did; but those transgress a precept of Christ, who deny or withhold due support.
[1Cor.9.15-1Cor.9.23]
Verses 15-23
It is the glory of a minister to deny himself, that he may serve Christ and save souls. But when a minister gives up his right for the sake of the gospel, he does more than his charge and office demands. By preaching the gospel, freely, the apostle showed that he acted from principles of zeal and love, and thus enjoyed much comfort and hope in his soul. And though he looked on the ceremonial law as a yoke taken off by Christ, yet he submitted to it, that he might work upon the Jews, do away their prejudices, prevail with them to hear the gospel, and win them over to Christ. Though he would transgress no laws of Christ, to please any man, yet he would accommodate himself to all men, where he might do it lawfully, to gain some. Doing good was the study and business of his life; and, that he might reach this end, he did not stand on privileges. We must carefully watch against extremes, and against relying on any thing but trust in Christ alone. We must not allow errors or faults, so as to hurt others, or disgrace the gospel.
[1Cor.9.24-1Cor.9.27]
Verses 24-27
The apostle compares himself to the racers and combatants in the Isthmian games, well known by the Corinthians. But in the Christian race all may run so as to obtain. There is the greatest encouragement, therefore, to persevere with all our strength, in this course. Those who ran in these games were kept to a spare diet. They used themselves to hardships. They practised the exercises. And those who pursue the interests of their souls, must combat hard with fleshly lusts. The body must not be suffered to rule. The apostle presses this advice on the Corinthians. He sets before himself and them the danger of yielding to fleshly desires, pampering the body, and its lusts and appetites. Holy fear of himself was needed to keep an apostle faithful: how much more is it needful for our preservation! Let us learn from hence humility and caution, and to watch against dangers which surround us while in the body.

Israel's privileges did not guarantee salvation (verses 1–5)

Paul reminded the Corinthians of the ancient Israelites to warn them against fellowship with idolaters and false confidence while continuing in sin.

Through a miracle Israel passed through the Red Sea, while the Egyptians pursuing them drowned.

That passage was a type of baptism.

The manna with which God fed the people pictured Christ crucified, the Bread from heaven. Everyone who receives him truly will live forever.

Christ is the Rock on which the Christian church is built.

From him streams of spiritual refreshment flow to believers, picturing the Holy Spirit's gracious work through Christ.

Yet Israel's privileges did not prevent judgment upon unbelief and sin.

Neither possession of religious privileges nor a profession of truth can secure heavenly happiness for someone whose heart remains unconverted.

Learn from Israel's sins and God's faithful protection (verses 6–14)

Sinful appetites grow stronger when they are indulged.

Therefore, restrain them as soon as they arise.

If we want to avoid Israel's judgments, we should fear falling into its sins.

Those who deliberately tempt Christ may be left under the power of the ancient serpent, their enemy.

Complaining against God's providential dealings and his commands greatly offends him.

Nothing written in Scripture is useless.

We are obligated to learn from its warnings.

Others have fallen; we may fall too.

A Christian's protection against sin includes distrusting personal strength and self-confidence.

God has not promised to preserve us from falling while we neglect watchfulness.

But Paul's warning is joined to great encouragement.

Others have carried burdens and faced temptations like ours.

Through divine grace, we can also endure and overcome.

God is both wise and faithful.

He knows what we can bear and will not permit temptation to overwhelm his people beyond what he enables them to endure.

He will provide a way of escape.

That may mean removing the trial or preventing it from destroying us spiritually.

We have every reason to flee sin and remain faithful.

When we hold firmly to him, temptation cannot finally defeat us.

Whether the world smiles upon us or treats us harshly, it remains a danger.

Through Christ, believers are strengthened to resist both its threats and its enticements.

Reverence for the Lord, planted within the heart, is a great means of protection.

Idolatrous worship cannot be combined with Christ's table (verses 15–22)

Participating in the Lord's Supper is a public profession of faith in Christ crucified and grateful worship of him for his saving work.

Through this ordinance, believers express their unity in Christ.

Like grains gathered together in one loaf, or members forming one body, Christians share fellowship with Christ and with each other.

Paul confirms this meaning by referring to the Old Testament sacrifices.

Those eating from the sacrifices participated in the worship associated with the altar.

Similarly, eating food as part of an idol's sacrifice meant taking part in worship of that idol and having fellowship with what stood behind the idolatry.

A person cannot share communion with Christ and demons at the same time.

It would contradict Christianity itself.

Christians should also beware of places and occasions that encourage them to offer themselves to sinful bodily pleasures, the desires of their eyes or the pride of life.

Such conduct provokes God.

Use liberty for God's glory and others' good (verses 23–33)

Some food previously offered to idols could lawfully be eaten.

For example, meat given to a pagan priest might later be sold in a public market as ordinary food.

But believers must ask more than “Is this permitted?”

They must also ask “Is this beneficial and does it build up others?”

Christianity does not forbid ordinary kindness or justify rude conduct toward people who differ from us in their religious beliefs or practices.

The freedom to eat common food must, however, be distinguished from participating in a religious feast involving idol worship.

Christian liberty must never be exercised so carelessly that it harms others or brings unnecessary disgrace on us.

Whatever we eat, drink or do, we should do everything for God's glory, seeking to honor him.

This is religion's great purpose and a guide to conduct even where Scripture does not supply a detailed rule.

A holy, peaceable and generous spirit can overcome the hostility of even determined opponents.
